title: Venus Is Putting On a Double Sky Show This July—Here's How to Watch!
summary: Get ready for a double feature in the evening sky! Venus, the brightest planet, is about to put on two easy-to-see shows. You don't need a telescope—just your eyes and maybe some binoculars. First up, on July 9, Venus will slide right next to Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo the Lion. Regulus looks blue-white and marks the lion's heart. Venus will outshine it by 158 times! They'll be just one degree apart—that's about the width of your pinky finger held at arm's length. Look low in the western sky around 9:45 p.m. local time. You'll see Venus as a dazzling silvery dot, with fainter Regulus to its upper right. They'll be close from July 7 to 12, but July 9 is the tightest hug. Then, on July 17, the moon joins the party. A slender crescent moon, only 17% lit, will hang to the left of Venus. They won't be super close—about six degrees apart, or three finger-widths—but the pair will still look magical as they sink toward the horizon. With binoculars, you might catch "earthshine": sunlight bouncing off Earth that dimly lights the moon's dark side with a ghostly blue-gray glow. Venus has been climbing higher all year, but after mid-August it will start sinking lower. Catch it now while it's still easy to spot! By late September, it will be tricky to see, and then it disappears in October. But don't worry—it'll pop back up in the morning sky just in time for the holidays, like a brilliant "star in the east."
why_it_matters: Watching Venus and the moon together can be a magical family experience that sparks your curiosity about the night sky and space.

background_read: Venus is often called the 'Evening Star' because it appears so bright after sunset.
The constellation Leo the Lion (a group of stars shaped like a lion, one of the ancient patterns in the sky) is home to Regulus, which is not one star but four stars moving around each other!
Earthshine is the ghostly glow on the Moon first explained by artist and scientist Leonardo da Vinci.
Article_Structure: WHO: Venus, Regulus, the crescent moon, and skywatchers like you.
WHAT: Two close approaches in the sky: Venus near Regulus on July 9, then the moon near Venus on July 17.
WHERE: Low in the western sky around 9:45 p.m. local time.
WHY: Venus is in a favorable position now but will soon sink, so it's the best time to observe.

perspectives.description: Free sky events like this are thrilling to watch with just your eyes and can turn anyone into a space fan.
Simple planet-watching is an easy way to teach kids about the Solar System and how things move.
These close approaches help astronomers study the positions and motions of planets, refining our knowledge of orbits.
